text: Why the shift stops at $D_7$ (the pairing lemma). If $x^E\in\gamma_k$, $E=2^s\ge4$, then $E(x-1)\in\Delta^2$, $2E(x-1)\in\Delta^3$, $4E(x-1)\in\Delta^4$ (expand $x^E-1=\sum_m\binom Em(x-1)^m$; for the last step $4\binom E3=\frac{(E-1)(E-2)}3\cdot2E$ and $3\mid(E-1)(E-2)$). Hence $(x-1)(\zeta^{2^{k-2}E}-1)\in\Delta^{2k}$ for $\zeta\in\gamma_k$, $k\le4$: this is the factor $x_1^{16}=x_1^{2E_1}$, $x_2^{128}=x_2^{2E_2}$ in (3.14) ($k=3$). For class 5 ($k=4$) the analogue needs $g_i=\prod_jx_j^{L_{ij}}=\zeta_i^{4E_i}$, while (3.12) has $g_1=\zeta_1^{16}$, $g_2=\zeta_2^{128}$, i.e. $2E_i$. scripts/plateau5_pairing.py enumerates the power-of-2 scalings of $E_i$, of the rows of the exponent matrix and of $L_{ij}$ for which $g_i\in4E_iD$ modulo $\gamma_c$ (121 644 of them); the 80 cheapest, built at class 4, all have $w=1$ in $M$. In this family the two requirements are in tension: $w\ne1$ needs some $L_{ij}<E_iE_j$ (since $[x_j,x_i^{E_i}]$-type factors have order dividing $E_j$), and the quadrupled pairing pushes the $L_{ij}$ up.

text: Lemma 1 [on paper]. Let $Q$ be a finitely generated nilpotent group of class $\le3$ and $n\in\{4,5\}$. Then $D_n(Q)\subseteq\tau(\gamma_3(Q))$ (the torsion of $\gamma_3$), and $\theta:\gamma_3(Q)\to\Delta^3/\Delta^n$, $g\mapsto g-1$, is a homomorphism with kernel $D_n(Q)\cap\gamma_3(Q)$. Hence, if $\tau(\gamma_3(Q))$ is a 2-group, $D_n(Q)=1$ iff $\theta$ is injective on the elements of order 2 of $\tau(\gamma_3(Q))$. Proof. $D_3=\gamma_3$ for every group (classical, see [MP09, ch. 1] †), so $D_n(Q)\subseteq\gamma_3(Q)$. By Jennings the rational dimension subgroups are the isolators: $D_n(Q)\subseteq\sqrt{\gamma_n(Q)}=\tau(Q)$ for $n\ge4$ (Jennings 1955 †; the same fact as Quillen's theorem behind the certificate of §6.4). For $g,h\in\gamma_3$: $gh-1=(g-1)+(h-1)+(g-1)(h-1)$ and $(g-1)(h-1)\in\Delta^6$. A nontrivial subgroup of a finite 2-group contains an element of order 2. $\square$

text: Corollary 2 [on paper]. Let $G$ be a group with $\gamma_5(G)=1$ and $Q=G/\gamma_4(G)$ with $D_5(Q)=1$. Then $D_r(G)\cap\gamma_4(G)=1$ implies $D_r(G)=1$ for every $r\ge5$: the image of $D_r(G)$ in $Q$ lies in $D_r(Q)\subseteq D_5(Q)=1$.
